title: Syllabus
text:
Course description
This 2-credit course introduces basic concepts and methods for statistical learning, with an emphasis on modern health science applications. Topics include linear regression with regularization, supervised classification, unsupervised clustering, and dimensionality reduction. The target audience is second-year Biostatistics master’s students or early PhD students with interests in statistical learning techniques for health science data. Students will be trained with hands-on materials to understand the methods, implement the algorithms, and interpret results in real applications.

BIOST 2141, 2142, and 3011. Students are expected to have programming experience in R, or in a low-level language such as C, C++, Java, or Fortran. Prerequisites can be met with other relevant coursework or experience with consent from the instructor.

Quiz policy
A short 5-question quiz follows each of the 12 lecture topics, released on Canvas the same day as lecture and due before the next lecture. No late quizzes — the drop policy exists instead of a late-submission exception.


Homework policy
Five homework assignments, each covering two consecutive lecture topics (modules 2–11) — a mix of theory, simulation, and applied data analysis in R. Each is scoped to about 5 hours of work, released once both of its covered lectures have been taught and due two weeks later. Multiple hypothesis testing (module 12) has no homework, only its quiz. Submissions are electronic via Canvas. Discussion of homework with classmates is allowed, but each student must independently write and implement their own solution. title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
text:
In class we built support vector machines one idea at a time: a hyperplane that separates two classes, the maximal margin classifier that picks the widest such hyperplane, the soft margin that tolerates some violations, and kernels that bend the boundary. This lab lets you see each idea on simulated data. Move a hyperplane by hand, push support vectors around, turn the cost dial, switch kernels.
There is no code to run here. Each section is a small Shiny app that runs entirely in your browser (via Shinylive and webR) — no local R install needed. The first app takes 10–30 seconds to start while R and the packages download; the rest start faster after that.
The real data analysis — the tumor example from the slides and variable selection with the lasso — is in Lab 2.

section: A warning about C before we start
text:
A warning about C before we start
The slides (and ISLR) write the soft margin with a budget \(C\):
\[\sum_{i=1}^n \epsilon_i \le C .\]
A large budget means more tolerance for points on the wrong side of the margin — a wider margin.
Every R package we use (kernlab, e1071, caret) instead uses a cost C: the price paid per unit of violation. A large cost means less tolerance — a narrower margin. The two run in opposite directions:

software cost C




wider margin, more violations, more support vectors

small

small
large



Both labs use the software meaning. When you read C = 100 below, think “violations are expensive”, not “a big budget”. The apps fit SVMs with kernlab::ksvm(), the same engine caret’s svm* methods call in Lab 2.

title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
section: 1. A hyperplane is just a sign
text:
1. A hyperplane is just a sign
With \(p = 2\) features a hyperplane is a line, \(f(X) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 = 0\). The slides normalize \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1\); we build that in by writing \(\beta_1 = \cos\theta\), \(\beta_2 = \sin\theta\), so the two sliders are the direction of the normal vector (the angle \(\theta\)) and the offset \(\beta_0\).
The shading shows the sign of \(f(X)\). A point with label \(y_i = \pm 1\) is on the correct side when \(y_i f(x_i) > 0\). When every point is on the correct side, you have a separating hyperplane, and — because \(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 = 1\) — the smallest \(y_i f(x_i)\) is the margin \(M\): the distance from the line to the closest point.
Your job: find a separating hyperplane, then make \(M\) as large as you can. The title tells you the best achievable value.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

# Two well-separated clouds; y = -1 (lower left) and y = +1 (upper right)
set.seed(6)
n <- 20
sep <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  y  = rep(c(-1, 1), each = n))
grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 120),
                    X2 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 120))

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("theta", "angle θ (degrees)", min = 0, max = 355,
                value = 0, step = 5),
    sliderInput("beta0", "offset β₀", min = -5, max = 5,
                value = -2, step = 0.05)
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    # The hyperplane you chose (beta1^2 + beta2^2 = 1)
    b1 <- cos(input$theta * pi / 180)
    b2 <- sin(input$theta * pi / 180)
    f  <- input$beta0 + b1 * sep$X1 + b2 * sep$X2
    n_wrong <- sum(sep$y * f <= 0)
    M <- min(sep$y * f)
    grid$f <- input$beta0 + b1 * grid$X1 + b2 * grid$X2

    headline <- if (n_wrong == 0) {
      sprintf("Separating hyperplane!  Your margin M = %.2f", M)
    } else {
      sprintf("%d point(s) on the wrong side (circled)", n_wrong)
    }

    ggplot() +
      geom_raster(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, fill = f > 0), alpha = 0.25) +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = 0,
                   colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
      geom_point(data = sep, aes(X1, X2, colour = factor(y)), size = 3) +
      geom_point(data = sep[sep$y * f <= 0, ], aes(X1, X2), shape = 21,
                 size = 7, stroke = 1.2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#3B4992", `TRUE` = "#EE0000"),
                        labels = c("f(X) < 0", "f(X) > 0"), name = NULL,
                        drop = FALSE) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                          labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
      coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-0.5, 4.5), expand = FALSE) +
      labs(title = headline,
           subtitle = "best possible margin: M = 0.49") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
Notice how many different lines separate these two clouds — infinitely many. Separation alone does not pick a classifier; that is why we ask for the one with the largest margin. (Hint if you are stuck: the best angle is about 40° and the best offset about −2.75.)

title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
section: 2. The maximal margin classifier and its support vectors
text:
2. The maximal margin classifier and its support vectors
ksvm() with a linear kernel and a huge cost (C = 10000, so no violations are affordable) finds the maximal margin hyperplane for us. The solid line is the hyperplane; the dashed lines are the margins; circled points are the support vectors.
The slides claim the support vectors are the only points that matter. Test it: pick a point and slide it away from (positive) or toward (negative) the boundary. The grey line is the original hyperplane for comparison.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

set.seed(6)
n <- 20
sep <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1, 0.5), rnorm(n, 3, 0.5)),
                  y  = factor(rep(c(-1, 1), each = n)))

fit_mmc <- function(d) {
  ksvm(y ~ X1 + X2, data = d, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
       C = 10000, scaled = FALSE)
}
margin_M <- function(m) {                       # M = 1 / ||beta||
  w <- colSums(coef(m)[[1]] * xmatrix(m)[[1]])
  1 / sqrt(sum(w^2))
}

m0 <- fit_mmc(sep)
w0 <- colSums(coef(m0)[[1]] * xmatrix(m0)[[1]])
u  <- w0 / sqrt(sum(w0^2))                       # unit normal to the hyperplane
f0 <- predict(m0, sep, type = "decision")[, 1]

grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-0.5, 4.5, length.out = 150))
grid$f0 <- predict(m0, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("which_point", "Move",
                 c("a support vector", "a point far from the margin")),
    sliderInput("shift", "distance moved", min = -0.4, max = 1.5,
                value = 0, step = 0.05)
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    # Choose the point: the first support vector, or the point farthest from the line
    i <- if (input$which_point == "a support vector") alphaindex(m0)[[1]][1] else
      which.max(abs(f0))

    # Move it along the normal: positive = away from the boundary
    moved <- sep
    moved[i, c("X1", "X2")] <- sep[i, c("X1", "X2")] + input$shift * sign(f0[i]) * u
    m1 <- fit_mmc(moved)

    grid$f1 <- predict(m1, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]
    sv <- moved[alphaindex(m1)[[1]], ]

    ggplot() +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f0), breaks = 0,
                   colour = "grey60", linewidth = 1) +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f1), breaks = 0,
                   colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f1), breaks = c(-1, 1),
                   colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(data = moved, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 3) +
      geom_point(data = sv, aes(X1, X2), shape = 21, size = 7, stroke = 1.2) +
      geom_point(data = moved[i, ], aes(X1, X2), shape = 4, size = 5, stroke = 2) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                          labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
      coord_equal(xlim = c(-0.5, 4.5), ylim = c(-0.5, 4.5), expand = FALSE) +
      labs(title = sprintf("Margin M = %.2f (was %.2f)   |   %d support vectors",
                           margin_M(m1), margin_M(m0), length(alphaindex(m1)[[1]])),
           subtitle = "x marks the point you are moving") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
What you should see:

Far-away point: slide it anywhere in its range — the hyperplane does not move at all. It is not a support vector, so it has no say.
Support vector, pulled toward the boundary (negative): the margin shrinks immediately. The whole classifier is at the mercy of this one point.
Support vector, pushed away (positive): the margin widens until another point takes over as a support vector.

That sensitivity is the maximal margin classifier’s weakness, and the reason the soft margin exists.

title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
section: 3. The soft margin: turning the cost dial
text:
3. The soft margin: turning the cost dial
Now the classes overlap, so no separating hyperplane exists. The soft margin lets some points sit inside the margin, or even on the wrong side of the hyperplane. Slide the cost from cheap (left) to expensive (right), or press ▶ under the slider to sweep it automatically.

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

set.seed(3)
n <- 50
ovl <- data.frame(X1 = c(rnorm(n, 1.2, 0.8), rnorm(n, 2.8, 0.8)),
                  X2 = c(rnorm(n, 1.2, 0.8), rnorm(n, 2.8, 0.8)),
                  y  = factor(rep(c(-1, 1), each = n)))
grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-1.5, 5.5, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-1.5, 5.5, length.out = 150))

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("log10C", "log₁₀(cost C)", min = -2, max = 2,
                value = 0, step = 0.25,
                animate = animationOptions(interval = 1200))
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    C <- 10^input$log10C
    m <- ksvm(y ~ X1 + X2, data = ovl, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
              C = C, scaled = FALSE)
    w <- colSums(coef(m)[[1]] * xmatrix(m)[[1]])
    grid$f <- predict(m, grid, type = "decision")[, 1]
    sv <- ovl[alphaindex(m)[[1]], ]

    ggplot() +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = 0,
                   colour = "black", linewidth = 1) +
      geom_contour(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, z = f), breaks = c(-1, 1),
                   colour = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
      geom_point(data = ovl, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 2.5) +
      geom_point(data = sv, aes(X1, X2), shape = 21, size = 5, stroke = 0.8) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                          labels = c("y = -1", "y = +1"), name = NULL) +
      coord_equal(xlim = c(-1.5, 5.5), ylim = c(-1.5, 5.5), expand = FALSE) +
      labs(title = sprintf("cost C = %.2f   |   margin width = %.2f",
                           C, 2 / sqrt(sum(w^2))),
           subtitle = sprintf("%d support vectors (circled)   |   training error = %.0f%%",
                              nSV(m), 100 * error(m))) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

Cheap violations → wide margin, many support vectors. 70 of the 100 points help set the boundary, so no single point can drag it around: low variance, higher bias.
Expensive violations → narrow margin, few support vectors. The fit bends to a handful of points near the boundary: low bias, higher variance.
Training error barely changes (4% → 3%). So training error cannot pick C for us — it will always favor expensive violations. We choose C the way we choose every tuning parameter: cross-validation. That is exactly what caret::train() does in Lab 2.

title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
section: 4. Kernels: when a straight line won’t do
text:
4. Kernels: when a straight line won’t do
Here class +1 sits inside a ring and class -1 outside it — no straight line can separate them. We fit on 200 training points and report the error on 1,000 fresh test points from the same process. Try each kernel; for the radial kernel, also slide \(\gamma\) (kernlab calls it sigma).
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 680
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

make_ring <- function(n, noise) {
  X1 <- runif(n, -2, 2)
  X2 <- runif(n, -2, 2)
  inside <- sqrt(X1^2 + X2^2) + rnorm(n, 0, noise) < 1.2
  data.frame(X1, X2, y = factor(ifelse(inside, 1, -1), levels = c(-1, 1)))
}
grid <- expand.grid(X1 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 150),
                    X2 = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 150))
ring_colours <- scale_colour_manual(
  values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
  labels = c("y = -1 (outside)", "y = +1 (inside)"), name = NULL)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    selectInput("kern", "kernel",
                c("linear", "polynomial, degree 2", "polynomial, degree 3",
                  "radial")),
    conditionalPanel(
      "input.kern == 'radial'",
      sliderInput("log10gamma", "log₁₀(γ)", min = -1, max = 2,

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  ring_train <- reactive({ set.seed(4); make_ring(200, input$noise) })
  ring_test  <- reactive({ set.seed(5); make_ring(1000, input$noise) })

  output$fit_plot <- renderPlot({
    d <- ring_train()
    gamma <- 10^input$log10gamma
    m <- switch(input$kern,
      "linear"               = ksvm(y ~ ., d, kernel = "vanilladot",
                                    kpar = list(), C = 1),
      "polynomial, degree 2" = ksvm(y ~ ., d, kernel = "polydot",
                                    kpar = list(degree = 2), C = 1),
      "polynomial, degree 3" = ksvm(y ~ ., d, kernel = "polydot",
                                    kpar = list(degree = 3), C = 1),
      "radial"               = ksvm(y ~ ., d, kernel = "rbfdot",
                                    kpar = list(sigma = gamma), C = 1))

    train_err <- mean(predict(m, d) != d$y)
    test_err  <- mean(predict(m, ring_test()) != ring_test()$y)
    grid$pred <- predict(m, grid)

    ggplot() +
      geom_raster(data = grid, aes(X1, X2, fill = pred), alpha = 0.25) +
      geom_point(data = d, aes(X1, X2, colour = y), size = 2) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = c(`-1` = "#3B4992", `1` = "#EE0000"),
                        guide = "none") +
      ring_colours +
      coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
      labs(title = sprintf("%s%s", input$kern,
                           if (input$kern == "radial") sprintf(" (γ = %.2f)", gamma) else ""),
           subtitle = sprintf("training error %.1f%%   |   test error %.1f%%",
                              100 * train_err, 100 * test_err)) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)

  output$enlarged_plot <- renderPlot({
    d <- ring_train()
    ggplot(d, aes(X1^2, X2^2, colour = y)) +
      geom_point(size = 2) +
      geom_abline(intercept = 1.44, slope = -1, linetype = "dashed") +
      ring_colours +
      labs(x = expression(X[1]^2), y = expression(X[2]^2),
           title = "The ring becomes (almost) linearly separable",
           subtitle = "dashed line: X1² + X2² = 1.44, the true boundary") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

Things worth remembering

The margin is decided by a few points. Only the support vectors shape the SVM; everything else could move (within limits) without changing the fit.
Cost C in software is the opposite of the budget \(C\) on the slides. Large software C = expensive violations = narrow margin = low bias, high variance. Tune it by cross-validation, never by training error.
Kernels buy flexibility, and flexibility has to be earned. On the ring a degree-2 kernel is exactly right; when the labels themselves are noisy, no kernel helps.
Multi-class SVMs are a vote. kernlab fits one binary SVM per pair of classes.

text:
A note on caret
Following Lab 3, every model goes through caret::train() with one shared interface. We change the method argument and nothing else: "lda", "qda", "nb", "knn". The same cross-validation settings and the same centering/scaling apply to all four, so a difference in the results is a difference between the methods, not between how we called them.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
The data: Wisconsin breast tumors
The Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer (WDBC) dataset records 569 tumors from fine-needle-aspirate images. Each tumor is labeled Benign or Malignant — a binary outcome, so the ROC curve and AUC work directly. Ten features are measured (radius, texture, smoothness, and so on); for each feature the data gives its mean, standard error, and “worst” value across the image, for 30 columns in all.








About 63% of the tumors are benign and 37% malignant — imbalanced, but not severely. Keep that split in mind: a classifier that called everything benign would already be 63% accurate while catching zero cancers (so accuracy alone will not be enough to track performance, we need to look at other metrics).

Choosing the features
The full 30 features separate the two classes almost perfectly (test AUC near 0.98 - take my word for it although you are free to check :)). Every method would look great and we would learn nothing about their differences; so we deliberately keep a harder subset: four features, each in its mean and standard-error form.










Train / test split








createDataPartition keeps the benign/malignant ratio the same in both parts. We tune and fit on the 427 training tumors and judge every model on the same 142 held-out test tumors.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
Fitting the four models
The shared control object below asks for 10-fold cross-validation and, because we will want predicted probabilities for the ROC curve, class probabilities.









LDA and QDA
LDA assumes a single shared covariance matrix across classes (linear boundary); QDA gives each class its own (quadratic boundary). Same call, one argument apart.










Naive Bayes
Naive Bayes keeps the generative recipe but assumes the features are independent within each class — a diagonal covariance. Here we use the Gaussian version (usekernel = FALSE), matching the density in the slides (but remember, Naive Bayes is the ONLY generative model that allows for mixed data types!)
The suppressWarnings() wrapper hides a harmless “numerical 0 probability” message: on a few outlying tumors the Gaussian density underflows to zero. It does not affect the fit. Note that technically Naive Bayes could have other distributions to support feature space as well!










k-Nearest Neighbors
k-NN is non-parametric — no distribution assumed. We let cross-validation pick k from the odd numbers 1 to 25. This is the heaviest cell; give it a moment.








Cross-validation chooses k = 15 — not k = 1. That matches the slide’s warning: a very small k overfits (low bias, high variance), so CV pulls us toward a smoother boundary.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
Evaluating on the test set
The confusion matrix from the slides, in code. We set positive = "Malignant" because catching cancer is the outcome we care about, so sensitivity = “of the true malignant tumors, how many did we catch?” and specificity = “of the true benign tumors, how many did we correctly clear?”








Read the output against the slides: Accuracy is the overall proportion correct, Sensitivity and Specificity are the two class-wise rates, and Youden’s J = Sensitivity + Specificity − 1 summarizes both in one number.
Now the other three:

























Putting the four side by side








Three things worth reading off this table:

QDA beats LDA (accuracy 0.838 vs 0.817, Youden’s J 0.650 vs 0.593). The two classes really do have different covariance structure, so letting each class keep its own — the quadratic boundary — pays off. This is the QDA lesson from the slides, made concrete.
Naive Bayes is the weakest here (accuracy 0.782). Its independence assumption is wrong: these tumor measurements are correlated, and throwing the correlations away costs accuracy. A reminder that “naive” is a real assumption, not a free lunch.
k-NN and QDA tie on accuracy, but they get there differently: k-NN has the highest specificity (0.910 — best at clearing benign tumors) while QDA has the highest sensitivity (0.774 — best at catching cancer). In a screening setting a missed malignancy is the costly error, which would push you toward QDA even at equal accuracy.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
The ROC curve
Accuracy and the confusion matrix fix a single threshold (predict “Malignant” when its probability exceeds 0.5). The ROC curve sweeps every threshold, plotting sensitivity against 1 − specificity, and AUC is the area under it. Let’s draw all four on one plot.








A curve closer to the top-left corner is better. LDA and k-NN have the highest AUC (~0.90), even though QDA had the best single-threshold accuracy — a good illustration that “best classifier” depends on whether you care about one threshold or the whole range.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
Try it yourself
The comparison above used set.seed(2155). Does the winner depend on that particular split? Change the seed, re-run the split and the four fits, and see whether the ranking holds.








Across most splits QDA stays ahead of LDA on this feature set — the covariance difference is a property of the data, not an accident of one split.
For a second experiment: the lab uses eight features. Add radius_mean and area_mean to the soft vector near the top, re-run everything, and watch every model’s accuracy jump — those two features carry most of the signal, which is exactly why we left them out to keep the comparison interesting.

title: Class 5/Lab 1: Classifying Breast Tumors
text:
Things worth remembering

One interface, four methods. train(method = ...) let us swap LDA, QDA, naive Bayes, and k-NN without relearning four APIs.
The covariance assumption is the dial. LDA (shared) → QDA (per-class) → naive Bayes (diagonal) are the same generative idea under different restrictions, and on this data QDA’s extra flexibility earned its keep while naive Bayes’ independence assumption cost it.
Accuracy is not the whole story. Sensitivity, specificity, Youden’s J, and AUC each answer a different question, and for a cancer screen the one that matters most is sensitivity.

text:
The data: wages
We use the Wage dataset — 3,000 male workers from the Mid-Atlantic region, surveyed between 2003 and 2009. These are the same data behind the figures in today’s slides.
The question is one about labor economics: how does wage vary with age? We expect earnings to rise through early career, plateau in middle age, and decline near retirement. That shape is not a straight line, which makes this a natural place to relax the linearity assumption.







Variable

logwage

Two features of these data are worth noting before we model them.








region has a single level — every worker is from the Middle Atlantic region. It carries no information and cannot be used as a predictor. This is common in real survey extracts, and it is worth checking before you put a variable into a model.








There is a small group of very high earners. They show up as a separate cloud in the scatterplot below, and they are the reason the fitted curve sits below the visual “middle” of the points at some ages.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
section: Part 1: Where the linear model fails
text:
Part 1: Where the linear model fails
Fit a straight line and look at what it misses.
















Interpretation: the linear fit slopes gently upward across the whole age range. The LOESS curve shows what is actually happening: wages rise steeply from 18 to about 40, flatten through middle age, and fall after 60. The straight line splits the difference and describes none of the three phases.
The slope coefficient is statistically significant, so a purely mechanical reading of the output would call this a good model. The plot says otherwise. Everything that follows is a way of giving the model enough flexibility to follow that shape.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
text:
Part 2: Polynomial regression
The first idea from the slides: add powers of the predictor and keep using linear regression.
\[y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \beta_2 x_i^2 + \cdots + \beta_d x_i^d + \epsilon_i\]








Interpretation: the jump from linear to quadratic is highly significant — the curvature is real. The cubic term adds a little. The fourth-degree term adds almost nothing. This matches the guidance on the slides that \(d \leq 4\) is usually enough.









The tail problem
The slides warn that polynomials have “notorious tail behavior.” Here is what that means concretely. We ask the model to predict past the edge of the data, where nobody is older than 80.








Interpretation: the predicted wage falls off a cliff past age 80. The polynomial has no information out there, and a degree-4 curve that bends to fit the middle of the data must keep bending at the ends. This is the single biggest practical objection to polynomial regression, and it motivates everything in the next two sections.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
text:
Part 3: Step functions
A different idea: stop assuming any global shape. Cut the range of age into bins and fit a separate mean in each.
















Each coefficient is the difference in mean wage between that bin and the first (youngest) bin.








Interpretation: the fit is now completely local — no global shape is imposed. But it is flat inside each bin and jumps at the boundaries. Wages do not actually jump by several thousand dollars on a worker’s 33rd birthday. As the slides put it, unless there are natural breakpoints in the predictor, piecewise-constant functions miss the trend.
This suggests the obvious fix, which is also the slides’ question: what if we fit local polynomials within bins instead of local means?

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
section: Part 4: From piecewise polynomials to splines
text:
Part 4: From piecewise polynomials to splines
Fitting a separate cubic in each region gives flexibility, but nothing forces the pieces to meet. The result is discontinuous — and, as the slides note, hard to explain to anyone who has to act on the prediction.
Splines solve this by adding constraints at the knots: continuity of the function, then of its first derivative, then of its second. Each constraint costs flexibility and buys smoothness.








The basis has 6 columns: a cubic spline with \(K\) knots uses \(K + 3\) basis functions, plus the intercept. This is the key idea from the slides — once the basis is built, we are doing ordinary linear regression on transformed columns.
















Interpretation: the curve passes through the knots with no visible kink. The continuity constraints are doing their job — the fit is flexible where the data demand it and smooth everywhere.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
section: Part 5: Natural splines and the boundary
text:
Part 5: Natural splines and the boundary
A cubic spline is still a cubic near the edges, so it can swing just as badly as a polynomial there. A natural spline adds one more constraint: the function must be linear beyond the boundary knots.









Comparing confidence intervals at the edges
The slides claim natural splines give narrower confidence intervals at the boundary. Check it directly.








Interpretation: in the middle of the data the two are comparable. At age 80 the cubic spline’s interval is roughly twice as wide. The linearity constraint at the boundary is what buys that precision — the natural spline is not free to curve wildly where the data are thin, so its predictions there are more stable.
This is the same lesson as the polynomial tail problem, now with a principled fix rather than a warning.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
text:
Part 6: Local regression (LOESS)
Splines fix knots in advance. Local regression takes a different route: for each target point, fit a weighted regression using only nearby observations. The tuning parameter is span, the fraction of the data counted as “near.”
















Interpretation: enp is the equivalent number of parameters — how many degrees of freedom the fit effectively spends. A span of 0.1 spends about 33; a span of 0.8 spends under 5. That is the bias-variance tradeoff from the slides in one number. The small-span curve chases local noise (low bias, high variance); the large-span curve is smooth and may miss real structure (higher bias, lower variance).
Note also the pitfall the slides raise: LOESS needs observations near every target point, so it degrades quickly once you have more than about four predictors. With one predictor and 3,000 observations we are in a comfortable regime.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
text:
Part 7: Generalized additive models
Everything so far used a single predictor. GAMs extend the idea to many, modeling the outcome as a sum of smooth functions:
\[y_i = \beta_0 + f_1(x_{i1}) + f_2(x_{i2}) + \cdots + f_p(x_{ip}) + \epsilon_i\]
Each \(f_j\) can be a spline, a LOESS fit, or anything smooth. The model is fit by backfitting: cycle through the predictors, updating each function against the partial residuals from the others, until nothing changes.









Reading the output








This table is the most useful thing in the lab. The edf column is the effective degrees of freedom for each smooth term, and it tells you how non-linear each relationship turned out to be:

s(age) has edf near 5 — strongly curved, exactly the rise-plateau-decline shape we have been chasing all along.
s(year) has edf equal to 1 — the smoother collapsed to a straight line on its own. Wages drifted up linearly over 2003–2009, and the model discovered that no flexibility was needed.

An edf of 1 means “a line was enough.” You did not have to decide in advance which predictors needed curvature; the fit worked it out. That is the practical payoff of GAMs over manually choosing a polynomial degree or knot placement for every variable.








Interpretation: each panel shows one predictor’s contribution with the others held fixed. The age panel reproduces the familiar career arc. The year panel is a straight line with a gentle upward slope, consistent with its edf of 1.
The parametric terms are read as ordinary regression coefficients:








Education shows a clear gradient — each step up the ladder adds to expected wage, with the largest jump at an advanced degree. Information-sector jobs pay more than industrial ones. These are interpretable in exactly the way a linear model’s coefficients are, which is the balance the slides describe: flexibility where it is needed, interpretability where it is not.

title: Class 4/Lab1: Non-linear Regression, Splines, and GAMs
text:
Part 8: Putting it together
Compare every method on the same data. Because these are not all nested models, we compare them on cross-validated error rather than by hypothesis test.








Interpretation. Three things stand out.
First, every non-linear method beats the straight line, confirming what the opening plot showed.
Second, among the single-predictor methods the differences are small. Polynomial, spline, and natural spline all land close together. They are different ways of buying the same flexibility, and on this dataset they buy about the same amount. The step function trails because it cannot follow a trend inside a bin.
Third, the GAM is clearly ahead — but that is not a fair fight on flexibility alone. It wins because it uses education, jobclass, and year in addition to age. Age is genuinely informative, and so is the rest of the model.

ImportantThings worth remembering

Ask what happens past the edge of the data. Polynomials fail badly there; natural splines are built to fail gracefully.
Let the model tell you how much flexibility it needs. The edf from a GAM is more honest than a degree you guessed in advance.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
The data: prostate cancer
The dataset has 97 men who were about to undergo radical prostatectomy. The outcome is logPSA, the log of prostate-specific antigen — the blood marker used to monitor prostate cancer.
The clinical question is one a biostatistician is often asked: which tumor characteristics explain PSA, and can we predict it from a smaller set of measurements? This matters in practice because the predictors differ in cost. Age is free. Cancer volume and Gleason score require a biopsy.







Variable
Clinical meaning




lcavol
log cancer volume — how much tumor is present


lweight
log prostate weight


age
patient age in years


lbph
log benign prostatic hyperplasia — non-cancerous enlargement


svi
seminal vesicle invasion (0/1) — tumor has spread beyond the prostate


lcp
log capsular penetration — tumor breaching the prostate capsule


gleason
Gleason score (6–9) — biopsy grade, how aggressive the cells look


pgg45
percent of biopsy tissue that is Gleason grade 4 or 5



















Note that svi is binary — only 21 of 97 men had seminal vesicle invasion. Keep that in mind when we interpret its coefficient.

One shared cross-validation setup
Every model in this lab uses the same resampling scheme, defined once:














NoteOn the choice of 10-fold CV



With only 97 observations, a single 10-fold split is noisy — each held-out fold has about 10 patients, so the estimated error moves around depending on the random split. Results can shift if you change the seed.
For a more stable estimate, use repeated cross-validation:
ctrl_repeated <- trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 5)
This runs the whole 10-fold procedure 5 times with different splits and averages the results. We use plain 10-fold here to keep the lab fast in the browser. Try swapping in ctrl_repeated at the end and see how much the selected models change.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
Part 1: Linear regression baseline
Start with the single strongest predictor. Cancer volume has the highest correlation with PSA, which is what a clinician would expect — more tumor produces more PSA.
































Now fit the full model with all eight predictors and compare.








Adding seven predictors improves cross-validated RMSE from about 0.78 to about 0.74. The gain is small compared to the number of parameters we spent to get it. That gap is what the rest of the lab is about.

A warning sign in the coefficients








Look at lcp (capsular penetration). Its coefficient is negative. Now check its correlation with the outcome on its own:








Both variables flip sign. On its own, capsular penetration is strongly and positively associated with PSA (r = 0.55). In the full model its coefficient is negative.
What you would tell the clinician: capsular penetration does raise PSA. But it travels closely with cancer volume (r = 0.68) and seminal vesicle invasion (r = 0.67). Once the model already knows those two things, lcp has nothing left to explain, and its coefficient is determined by noise. The sign flip is a symptom of correlated predictors, not a claim that capsular penetration protects against high PSA.








This is exactly the instability that shrinkage methods are built to control. Note that gleason and pgg45 are correlated at 0.75 — we return to that pair in Part 3.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
Part 2: Subset selection
Rather than keeping all eight predictors, choose a subset. We compare three search strategies, all through the same train() interface:

leapSeq — best subset (exhaustive search)
leapForward — forward stepwise
leapBackward — backward stepwise

The tuning parameter nvmax is the number of predictors allowed in the model.








All three strategies agree: about three predictors. For a small predictor set like this one the three methods often agree, but that is not guaranteed. Forward and backward selection are greedy — they commit to one variable at a time and can miss the subset that exhaustive search would find.

Which variables enter at each size?
caret reports cross-validated error, but it does not show the entry order. For that we call regsubsets() directly.








Each row is a model size; each * marks an included predictor. Read down the first column: lcavol enters first and never leaves. Then lweight, then svi. These are the same three predictors the cross-validation chose.










Choosing a model size by information criteria
Cross-validation is one way to pick the size. The classical alternative is a penalized criterion computed on the training fit.
























Interpretation: RSS always decreases as you add predictors, so it always picks the largest model and cannot be used to choose a size. That is why the other three criteria exist — each penalizes complexity differently.
The criteria disagree here: BIC picks 3, Cp picks 5, adjusted \(R^2\) picks 7. That disagreement is the lesson. BIC penalizes complexity most heavily, so it gives the smallest model. There is no single correct answer; the choice depends on whether you want a parsimonious model to explain to a clinician or the best possible predictive fit.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
section: Part 3: Ridge, lasso, and elastic net
text:
Part 3: Ridge, lasso, and elastic net
Subset selection makes a hard in-or-out decision for each predictor. Shrinkage methods instead pull all coefficients toward zero continuously, trading a small amount of bias for a large reduction in variance.
All three methods are the same glmnet model with a different mixing parameter \(\alpha\):

\(\alpha = 0\) — ridge, L2 penalty, shrinks coefficients but keeps all of them
\(\alpha = 1\) — lasso, L1 penalty, can set coefficients to exactly zero
\(0 < \alpha < 1\) — elastic net, a blend of both

caret tunes \(\alpha\) and \(\lambda\) together on one grid. We standardize the predictors with preProcess so the penalty applies fairly to variables measured on different scales.

























How the penalty changes what is kept
Fit each \(\alpha\) separately, letting each one choose its own best \(\lambda\), and compare the coefficients side by side.
















Interpretation. Ridge (\(\alpha = 0\)) keeps all eight predictors. As \(\alpha\) increases, more coefficients are driven to exactly zero. This is the practical difference between the two penalties: the L1 penalty has corners on the coordinate axes, so the solution can land exactly on zero. The L2 penalty is smooth and shrinks coefficients toward zero without reaching it.
Note that lcavol, lweight, and svi keep large coefficients at every value of \(\alpha\). These are the same three predictors subset selection chose. Tumor burden and spread beyond the prostate drive PSA, and every method agrees.


The grouping effect: gleason and pgg45
Look at the gleason row of the coefficient table above as \(\alpha\) increases.








These two variables measure the same clinical concept. Both come from the same biopsy and both grade how aggressive the tumor cells look — gleason is the summary score, pgg45 is the percentage of high-grade tissue. They correlate at 0.75.








What you would tell the clinician. Ridge keeps both markers and splits the credit between them (0.050 and 0.085). As \(\alpha\) rises, gleason shrinks steadily — 0.022, then 0.010, then 0.0001 — until the lasso sets it to zero, while pgg45 stays near 0.06 throughout. If the urologist asks why the model discarded the Gleason score, the answer is that pgg45 already carries the same information, and the lasso was forced to choose one of the two. Tumor grade still matters for PSA — the model simply measures it through the other variable.
The important caution is that this choice is driven by noise. With a different sample of 97 patients, the lasso might keep gleason and drop pgg45 instead. When you read a paper reporting a lasso-selected biomarker panel, this is the reason to be careful about which specific markers made the list.
Elastic net sits between the two extremes. It shrinks correlated predictors toward each other instead of forcing a hard choice, so groups of related markers tend to stay in or drop out together. This is the behavior that makes it a sensible default when predictors come in clinically related clusters.








lcp is set to zero by every method with \(\alpha > 0\). The unstable, sign-flipped coefficient from the OLS fit is removed by the penalty. This is shrinkage doing the job it was designed for.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
Part 4: Partial least squares
Subset selection and shrinkage both work on the original predictors. Dimension reduction takes a different route: build a small number of new variables as combinations of the originals, then regress on those.
Partial least squares constructs components that explain variance in the predictors and correlate with the outcome.
















Interpretation: most of the predictive signal is captured by about three components. Adding more components does not improve cross-validated error, because the later components describe directions in the predictor space that carry little information about PSA.
Three components, three predictors from subset selection, three large coefficients under the lasso. All three approaches point at the same conclusion — this problem has roughly three dimensions of useful signal.
The tradeoff is interpretability. A PLS component is a weighted combination of all eight predictors, so you cannot tell the clinician “drop the Gleason score from the panel.” You can only say “this combination predicts well.”








Reading the first component: it loads heavily on lcavol, lcp, and svi — all measures of tumor burden and spread. The component has a clinical meaning even though it is not a single measurement.

title: Class 3/Lab1: Subset Selection and Shrinkage
text:
Part 5: Putting it together
Compare every method on the same cross-validation folds.
















Interpretation. The methods land close together on this dataset. That is a realistic result — with 97 observations and 8 predictors, no method has much room to separate itself from the others, and the differences are within the noise of the cross-validation.
What differs is the kind of model each produces:








Method
Predictors used
Can explain to a clinician?

yes — a short, concrete list

The counts above come from the coefficient table in Part 3. Note that the lasso here drops two predictors rather than reducing to the three that subset selection chose — at its cross-validated \(\lambda\), the penalty is mild enough to retain small coefficients on age, lbph, and pgg45.
Choosing among them is a decision about what the model is for, not only about which has the lowest RMSE.






ImportantA caveat worth stating



This dataset has 97 patients. The three-predictor consensus is a finding within this sample, and the cross-validated differences between methods are small relative to their variability. Treat this lab as an illustration of how the methods behave, not as clinical evidence about PSA.
Try re-running the shrinkage section with set.seed(1) instead of set.seed(2155) and see which conclusions hold and which move.

title: Class 2/Lab1: Training, Evaluating, and Resampling Models
text:
In this lab, we will build the toolkit for training and evaluating statistical learning models. Every code cell below runs live in your browser via webR — no local R install needed. Edit any cell and re-run it to see what changes.
Packages load once when the page opens (see the webr: packages: list in the YAML front matter above) — give it a few seconds on first load.
Using simulated data, we will:

Calculate common performance metrics (RMSE, Accuracy, Silhouette Score, Explained Variance) by hand, so the formulas behind caret/yardstick output stop being a black box.
Fit polynomials of increasing degree to the same data and watch training error keep falling while test error eventually turns back up — the bias-variance tradeoff.
Use the bootstrap to estimate the standard error and a confidence interval for a statistic without relying on a textbook formula.




RMSE measures the average magnitude of the errors between predicted and actual values.
\[RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(predicted_i - actual_i)^2}\]
























Try it live: change set.seed(42) to a different number and re-run all three cells above — watch RMSE change.




Accuracy is the proportion of correct predictions among all cases evaluated — the most common classification metric, though it can be misleading on imbalanced data.
\[Accuracy = \frac{True\,Positives + True\,Negatives}{Total\,Samples}\]
























Live-coding demo: the blank marks the one piece of the accuracy formula left to fill in — true negatives, added alongside true positives in the numerator.




The silhouette score measures how similar a point is to its own cluster (cohesion) versus the nearest other cluster (separation). It ranges from -1 to +1; higher is better.
\[s(i) = \frac{b(i) - a(i)}{\max(a(i), b(i))}\]
where \(a(i)\) is the average distance from point \(i\) to other points in its own cluster, and \(b(i)\) is the average distance from \(i\) to points in the nearest neighboring cluster.
















Try it live: change centers = 2 to centers = 3 or 4 in the first cell and re-run both cells — watch the average silhouette score change as the clustering gets forced into the wrong number of groups.




In PCA, explained variance is the proportion of total variance captured by each principal component — used to decide how many components to keep.
























Try it live: change cov_matrix <- matrix(c(5, 4, 4, 5), nrow = 2) to matrix(c(5, 0, 0, 5), nrow = 2) (zero covariance) and re-run all three cells — watch the first component’s explained variance drop from dominant to about 50%, since the features are no longer correlated.




Here we generate data from a known nonlinear function, then fit polynomials of increasing degree and track training vs. test error. Low-degree models underfit (high bias); high-degree models overfit (high variance).
















Live-coding demo: fill in the blank with a low degree (e.g. 1) — model underfits. Re-run with a high degree (e.g. 10) — model overfits. This #| exercise: blank is the code-blanks pattern: everything else is given, only the one concept-defining value is left for the class to fill in live.








Interpretation: Training error decreases (almost) monotonically as we add flexibility — the model can always fit the training points more closely. Test error decreases at first as bias drops, then rises again once the model starts fitting noise instead of signal. The degree at which test error is minimized is the sweet spot in the bias-variance tradeoff for this dataset.




The bootstrap estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic by resampling the observed data with replacement, without relying on a closed-form formula for its standard error.
























Interpretation: The bootstrap SE and CI closely match what the Central Limit Theorem predicts for the mean of a normal sample (\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)), which is why the bootstrap is trustworthy here — and why it’s most useful for statistics (medians, correlations, model coefficients) where no such closed-form formula exists.
Try it live: change statistic_fn <- mean to statistic_fn <- sd or statistic_fn <- median and re-run both cells — the whole pipeline updates. The standard deviation’s bootstrap distribution is noticeably right-skewed in small samples, unlike the mean’s.

title: Class 6/Lab 1: Seeing Support Vector Machines
text:
5. More than two classes
SVMs are binary by construction. The slides gave two ways round that: one-versus-all (fit \(K\) classifiers, each class against the rest) and one-versus-one (fit all \(\binom{K}{2}\) pairwise classifiers and let them vote). kernlab uses one-versus-one. With three iris species that means \(\binom{3}{2} = 3\) binary SVMs inside one fitted model — the subtitle counts them from the fitted object.
The app shows the combined vote as three-colored decision regions. The two feature pairs give very different problems:
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(kernlab)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("features", "features", c("petal", "sepal")),
    radioButtons("kernel", "kernel", c("linear", "radial"))
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    vars <- if (input$features == "petal") c("Petal.Length", "Petal.Width") else
                                           c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width")
    d <- data.frame(x1 = iris[[vars[1]]], x2 = iris[[vars[2]]],
                    Species = iris$Species)

    set.seed(1)
    m <- if (input$kernel == "linear") {
      ksvm(Species ~ x1 + x2, data = d, kernel = "vanilladot", kpar = list(),
           C = 1, cross = 10)
    } else {
      ksvm(Species ~ x1 + x2, data = d, kernel = "rbfdot", C = 1, cross = 10)
    }

    grid <- expand.grid(x1 = seq(min(d$x1) - 0.3, max(d$x1) + 0.3, length.out = 150),
                        x2 = seq(min(d$x2) - 0.3, max(d$x2) + 0.3, length.out = 150))
    grid$pred <- predict(m, grid)
    species_cols <- c(setosa = "#3B4992", versicolor = "#EE0000",
                      virginica = "#008B45")

    ggplot() +
      geom_raster(data = grid, aes(x1, x2, fill = pred), alpha = 0.25) +
      geom_jitter(data = d, aes(x1, x2, colour = Species, shape = Species),
                  width = 0.03, height = 0.03, size = 2.5) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = species_cols) +
      scale_fill_manual(values = species_cols, guide = "none") +
      coord_cartesian(expand = FALSE) +
      labs(x = vars[1], y = vars[2],
           title = sprintf("%s kernel on %s features   |   10-fold CV error %.1f%%",
                           input$kernel, input$features, 100 * cross(m)),
           subtitle = sprintf("one-versus-one: %d pairwise classifiers in this model",
                              length(coef(m)))) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

Petal features: both kernels separate the three species almost perfectly (10-fold CV error 4.7% linear, 4.0% radial). Setosa sits far off on its own; the two classifiers that involve it are easy.
Sepal features: the error jumps to about 21% (linear) and 25% (radial). Versicolor and virginica overlap heavily on sepal measurements, and no kernel can separate points that sit on top of each other — the radial kernel just draws a more contorted boundary through the overlap and does worse. Better features beat a fancier kernel.

Things worth remembering

Cost C in software is the opposite of the budget \(C\) on the slides. Tune it by cross-validation on a log-spaced grid, never by training error.

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
section: 1. Lloyd’s algorithm, one step at a time
text:
1. Lloyd’s algorithm, one step at a time
The slides give the algorithm in two steps:

Randomly assign a number from 1 to \(K\) to each observation.
Repeat until the assignments stop changing:

Update: for each cluster, compute the centroid (the mean of its points).
Assign: move each observation to the cluster with the closest centroid.


Click Next step to do one half-step at a time. The title says which step just happened. The right panel tracks the within-cluster sum of squares (WSS), \(\sum_k \sum_{i \in C_k} \lVert x_i - \mu_k \rVert^2\), after every half-step. Here \(\mu_k\) is the current centroid of cluster \(k\) (the big X). Click New random start to begin again from a different random assignment.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 660
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
ctr <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(4, 0.5), c(1.5, 3.5))
pts <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(150, ctr[rep(1:3, each = 50), 1], 0.8),
                  x2 = rnorm(150, ctr[rep(1:3, each = 50), 2], 0.8))
X <- as.matrix(pts)
pal <- c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45", "#631879", "#E69F00")

centroids <- function(cl, K, old = NULL) {
  t(sapply(1:K, function(k) {
    if (any(cl == k)) colMeans(X[cl == k, , drop = FALSE])
    else if (!is.null(old)) old[k, ] else colMeans(X)   # keep an empty cluster's old centroid
  }))
}
wss_of <- function(cl, cen) sum((X - cen[cl, ])^2)

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("K", "number of clusters K", min = 2, max = 5, value = 3),
    actionButton("restart", "New random start"),
    actionButton("step", "Next step", class = "btn-primary"),
    actionButton("finish", "Run to the end")
  ),
  layout_columns(col_widths = c(7, 5),
    plotOutput("scatter", height = "560px"),
    plotOutput("trace", height = "560px"))
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  st <- reactiveValues()
  init <- function() {
    K <- input$K
    st$cl <- sample(1:K, nrow(X), replace = TRUE)       # step 1: random labels
    st$cen <- NULL
    st$next_is <- "update"
    st$iter <- 0
    st$msg <- "Start: random labels, no centroids yet"
    st$hist <- data.frame(step = 0, wss = wss_of(st$cl, centroids(st$cl, K)),
                          kind = "start")
    st$done <- FALSE
  }
  half_step <- function() {
    if (st$done) return()
    K <- input$K
    if (st$next_is == "update") {
      st$cen <- centroids(st$cl, K, st$cen)
      st$iter <- st$iter + 1
      st$msg <- sprintf("Iteration %d (a): update centroids", st$iter)
      st$next_is <- "assign"
      kind <- "update"
    } else {
      d <- sapply(1:K, function(k) colSums((t(X) - st$cen[k, ])^2))
      new_cl <- max.col(-d, ties.method = "first")
      changed <- sum(new_cl != st$cl)
      st$cl <- new_cl
      st$msg <- sprintf("Iteration %d (b): %d point(s) moved", st$iter, changed)
      st$next_is <- "update"
      if (changed == 0) { st$done <- TRUE; st$msg <- sprintf("Converged after %d iterations", st$iter) }
      kind <- "assign"
    }
    cen <- if (is.null(st$cen)) centroids(st$cl, K) else st$cen
    st$hist <- rbind(st$hist, data.frame(step = nrow(st$hist), wss = wss_of(st$cl, cen), kind = kind))
  }
  observeEvent(list(input$K, input$restart), init())
  observeEvent(input$step, half_step())
  observeEvent(input$finish, { for (i in 1:100) { if (st$done) break; half_step() } })

  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    req(st$cl)
    d <- cbind(pts, cluster = factor(st$cl, levels = 1:input$K))
    p <- ggplot(d, aes(x1, x2, colour = cluster)) +
      geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = pal, drop = FALSE) +
      coord_equal() +
      labs(title = st$msg,
           subtitle = sprintf("WSS = %.1f", tail(st$hist$wss, 1))) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    if (!is.null(st$cen)) {
      cd <- data.frame(x1 = st$cen[, 1], x2 = st$cen[, 2],
                       cluster = factor(1:input$K, levels = 1:input$K))
      p <- p + geom_point(data = cd, shape = 4, size = 9, stroke = 2.5)
    }
    p
  }, res = 96)

  output$trace <- renderPlot({
    req(st$hist)
    ggplot(st$hist, aes(step, wss)) +
      geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
      geom_point(aes(shape = kind), size = 3) +
      scale_shape_manual(values = c(start = 15, update = 16, assign = 17),
                         name = NULL) +
      labs(x = "half-step", y = "WSS", title = "WSS after each half-step") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
  }, res = 96)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
Things to notice:

The first update moves every centroid to the middle. Random labels mix all groups, so every cluster mean starts near the overall mean. The centroids then separate over the next few iterations.
WSS never goes up. Each half-step can only lower it, or leave it the same. The update step puts each centroid at the point that minimizes the sum of squares for its cluster. The assign step moves a point only when that makes its own term smaller. This is why the algorithm must stop.
Most of the gain comes early. The first two or three iterations do most of the work. The last iterations move a few points near the borders.
Set \(K = 5\) on data with three groups. The algorithm still runs and still converges. k-means always returns \(K\) clusters, even when \(K\) is wrong.

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
2. Bad starts and local minima
Lloyd’s algorithm stops when no single step helps. That is a local minimum. It is not always the best possible clustering. These data have five groups: two pairs on the left and one group on the right. The app runs kmeans() with \(K = 5\) from the random start you pick.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
ctr <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(3, 0), c(0, 5), c(3, 5), c(8, 2.5))
X <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, function(i)
  cbind(rnorm(40, ctr[i, 1], 0.6), rnorm(40, ctr[i, 2], 0.6))))
colnames(X) <- c("x1", "x2")
best <- kmeans(X, 5, nstart = 50)$tot.withinss
pal <- c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45", "#631879", "#E69F00")

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    sliderInput("seed", "random start number", min = 1, max = 30, value = 1,
                step = 1, animate = animationOptions(interval = 1500)),
    radioButtons("nstart", "nstart (starts per run, best one kept)",
                 choices = c(1, 5, 25), selected = 1, inline = TRUE)
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    set.seed(input$seed)
    km <- kmeans(X, 5, nstart = as.integer(input$nstart))
    worse <- 100 * (km$tot.withinss / best - 1)
    d <- data.frame(X, cluster = factor(km$cluster))
    cd <- data.frame(km$centers, cluster = factor(1:5))
    ggplot(d, aes(x1, x2, colour = cluster)) +
      geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
      geom_point(data = cd, shape = 4, size = 9, stroke = 2.5) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = pal) +
      coord_equal() +
      labs(title = sprintf("WSS = %.1f   (best possible: %.1f)", km$tot.withinss, best),
           subtitle = if (worse > 1) sprintf("Local minimum: %.0f%% worse than the best", worse)
                      else "This run found the best clustering") +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "none")
  }, res = 96)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
Press ▶ under the slider to step through the 30 starts. With nstart = 1:

20 of the 30 starts stop at a local minimum. A typical bad answer puts two centroids in one group and makes one centroid cover two groups.
With nstart = 5, 2 of the 30 runs are still bad. With nstart = 25, none are.

A local minimum looks like a normal result. kmeans() gives no warning. The only protection is many starts. Use nstart = 25 or more, and set a seed so that other people get the same clusters.

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
3. Units change the clusters
k-means uses Euclidean distance. A variable with a large spread contributes large distances, so it dominates. Below are 200 simulated patients, half with diabetes. Two lab values were measured:

HbA1c (%), which differs between the groups
total cholesterol, which does not differ between the groups

Cholesterol can be reported in mg/dL or in mmol/L (1 mmol/L = 38.67 mg/dL). The patients and the measurements stay the same. Only the units change.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 640
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
n <- 100
group <- factor(rep(c("no diabetes", "diabetes"), each = n),
                levels = c("no diabetes", "diabetes"))
chol_mgdl <- rnorm(2 * n, 200, 40)                     # same in both groups
a1c <- c(rnorm(n, 5.4, 0.35), rnorm(n, 7.6, 0.6))    # differs between groups

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("units", "cholesterol units",
                 choices = c("mg/dL", "mmol/L"), selected = "mg/dL"),
    checkboxInput("std", "standardize both variables first", FALSE),
    checkboxInput("equal", "draw both axes on the same scale (what k-means sees)", FALSE)
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    chol <- if (input$units == "mg/dL") chol_mgdl else chol_mgdl / 38.67
    X <- cbind(chol = chol, a1c = a1c)
    Xfit <- if (input$std) scale(X) else X
    set.seed(42)
    cl <- kmeans(Xfit, 2, nstart = 25)$cluster
    agree <- max(mean(cl == as.integer(group)), mean(cl != as.integer(group)))
    d <- data.frame(Xfit, cluster = factor(cl), group = group)
    p <- ggplot(d, aes(chol, a1c, colour = cluster, shape = group)) +
      geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.8) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c("#3B4992", "#EE0000")) +
      labs(x = if (input$std) "cholesterol (standardized)" else paste0("cholesterol (", input$units, ")"),
           y = if (input$std) "HbA1c (standardized)" else "HbA1c (%)",
           title = sprintf("k-means, K = 2: %.0f%% of patients matched to their group",
                           100 * agree)) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    if (input$equal) {
      # same units on both axes: centre the y-axis on the data, with the x-axis span
      span <- diff(range(d$chol)) / 2
      p <- p + coord_equal(xlim = range(d$chol), ylim = mean(d$a1c) + c(-span, span))
    }
    p
  }, res = 96)

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
4. Choosing \(K\)
Three tools from class and Lab 2:

Elbow: WSS against \(K\). Look for the bend.
Silhouette: for each point, compare the mean distance to its own cluster (\(a\)) with the mean distance to the nearest other cluster (\(b\)): \(s = (b - a)/\max(a, b)\). Choose the \(K\) with the largest mean \(s\). Lab 2 explains it in full.
Gap statistic: compare \(\log(\text{WSS})\) with its value on reference data with no clusters. Choose the smallest \(K\) whose gap is within one standard error of the next gap.

Pick a data set, change the spread of the groups, and see which \(K\) each tool picks. The left panel shows k-means with the \(K\) from the slider. The gap statistic uses \(B = 20\) reference sets, so give each change a few seconds.
#| '!! shinylive warning !!': |
#|   shinylive does not work in self-contained HTML documents.
#|   Please set `embed-resources: false` in your metadata.
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 760
library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)
library(cluster)

make_data <- function(type, spread) {
  set.seed(42)
  if (type == "no groups") return(cbind(x1 = rnorm(150), x2 = rnorm(150)))
  Kt <- if (type == "3 groups") 3 else 4
  ang <- 2 * pi * (1:Kt) / Kt
  y <- rep(1:Kt, each = 50)
  cbind(x1 = rnorm(50 * Kt, 3 * cos(ang)[y], spread),
        x2 = rnorm(50 * Kt, 3 * sin(ang)[y], spread))
}
pal <- c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45", "#631879", "#E69F00",
         "#008280", "#BB0021", "#5F559B")

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("type", "data", choices = c("3 groups", "4 groups", "no groups")),
    sliderInput("spread", "spread of each group (SD)", min = 0.5, max = 1.5,
                value = 0.5, step = 0.25),
    sliderInput("K", "K for the left panel", min = 1, max = 8, value = 3)
  ),
  layout_columns(col_widths = c(6, 6),
    plotOutput("scatter", height = "330px"),
    plotOutput("elbow", height = "330px"),
    plotOutput("sil", height = "330px"),
    plotOutput("gap", height = "330px"))
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  X <- reactive(make_data(input$type, input$spread))
  fits <- reactive({
    lapply(1:8, function(k) { set.seed(42); kmeans(X(), k, nstart = 10) })
  })
  sil <- reactive({
    d <- dist(X())
    sapply(2:8, function(k) mean(silhouette(fits()[[k]]$cluster, d)[, "sil_width"]))
  })
  gap <- reactive({
    set.seed(42)
    clusGap(X(), kmeans, K.max = 8, B = 20, nstart = 10)$Tab
  })
  base <- theme_bw(base_size = 14)
  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    d <- data.frame(X(), cluster = factor(fits()[[input$K]]$cluster))
    ggplot(d, aes(x1, x2, colour = cluster)) + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = pal) + coord_equal() +
      labs(title = sprintf("k-means with K = %d", input$K)) +
      base + theme(legend.position = "none")
  }, res = 96)
  output$elbow <- renderPlot({
    d <- data.frame(k = 1:8, wss = sapply(fits(), `[[`, "tot.withinss"))
    ggplot(d, aes(k, wss)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
      labs(x = "K", y = "WSS", title = "Elbow: look for the bend") + base
  }, res = 96)
  output$sil <- renderPlot({
    d <- data.frame(k = 2:8, s = sil())
    best <- d$k[which.max(d$s)]
    ggplot(d, aes(k, s)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
      geom_point(data = d[d$k == best, ], colour = "#EE0000", size = 4) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8, limits = c(1, 8)) +
      labs(x = "K", y = "average silhouette",
           title = sprintf("Silhouette picks K = %d", best)) + base
  }, res = 96)
  output$gap <- renderPlot({
    g <- gap()
    best <- maxSE(g[, "gap"], g[, "SE.sim"], method = "firstSEmax")
    d <- data.frame(k = 1:8, g)
    ggplot(d, aes(k, gap)) + geom_line() + geom_point(size = 2) +
      geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = gap - SE.sim, ymax = gap + SE.sim), width = 0.2) +
      geom_point(data = d[d$k == best, ], colour = "#EE0000", size = 4) +
      scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
      labs(x = "K", y = "Gap(K)", title = sprintf("Gap statistic picks K = %d", best)) + base
  }, res = 96)
}

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
5. Shapes that k-means cannot find
k-means puts each point with its closest centroid. So every cluster is a convex region around a centre, and the border between two clusters is a straight line halfway between their centroids. When the true groups have another shape, k-means cannot find them. Hierarchical clustering with a different linkage sometimes can.
Pick a shape and a method. \(K\) is set to the true number of groups. The title gives the share of points in a cluster that matches their true group.

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

make <- function(type) {
  set.seed(42)
  switch(type,
    "round, equal" = { y <- rep(1:3, each = 70)
      data.frame(x1 = rnorm(210, c(0, 4, 2)[y], 0.7), x2 = rnorm(210, c(0, 0, 3.5)[y], 0.7), g = y) },
    "unequal sizes" = { y <- rep(1:2, c(250, 30))
      data.frame(x1 = rnorm(280, c(0, 4.2)[y], c(1.2, 0.4)[y]), x2 = rnorm(280, 0, c(1.2, 0.4)[y]), g = y) },
    "elongated" = { y <- rep(1:2, each = 100)
      u <- rnorm(200, 0, 3); v <- rnorm(200, c(-1.1, 1.1)[y], 0.35)   # long along u, apart along v
      data.frame(x1 = (u - v) / sqrt(2), x2 = (u + v) / sqrt(2), g = y) },   # tilt by 45 degrees
    "rings" = { y <- rep(1:2, c(80, 160)); th <- runif(240, 0, 2 * pi)
      r <- c(1, 4)[y] + rnorm(240, 0, 0.25)
      data.frame(x1 = r * cos(th), x2 = r * sin(th), g = y) },
    "moons" = { y <- rep(1:2, each = 100); th <- runif(200, 0, pi)
      data.frame(x1 = ifelse(y == 1, cos(th), 1 - cos(th)) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.07),
                 x2 = ifelse(y == 1, sin(th), 0.5 - sin(th)) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.07), g = y) })
}
agree <- function(cl, g) { t <- table(cl, g); sum(apply(t, 1, max)) / length(g) }

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("type", "true groups",
                 choices = c("round, equal", "unequal sizes", "elongated", "rings", "moons")),
    radioButtons("method", "method",
                 choices = c("k-means", "hierarchical: complete", "hierarchical: average",
                             "hierarchical: single", "hierarchical: Ward"))
  ),
  plotOutput("plot", height = "560px")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  output$plot <- renderPlot({
    d <- make(input$type)
    X <- as.matrix(d[, c("x1", "x2")])
    K <- length(unique(d$g))
    cl <- if (input$method == "k-means") {
      set.seed(42); kmeans(X, K, nstart = 25)$cluster
    } else {
      link <- c("hierarchical: complete" = "complete", "hierarchical: average" = "average",
                "hierarchical: single" = "single", "hierarchical: Ward" = "ward.D2")[input$method]
      cutree(hclust(dist(X), method = link), K)
    }
    d$cluster <- factor(cl)
    ggplot(d, aes(x1, x2, colour = cluster)) +
      geom_point(size = 2.2, alpha = 0.8) +
      scale_colour_manual(values = c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45")) +
      coord_equal() +
      labs(title = sprintf("%s, K = %d: %.0f%% matched", input$method, K, 100 * agree(cl, d$g))) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "none")
  }, res = 96)
}

Round, equal groups are what k-means is built for. Every method except single linkage does well.
Unequal sizes: the k-means border sits halfway between the two centroids. The large, wide group reaches past that border, so k-means gives some of its points to the small group.
Elongated groups defeat every method here. Each group is a long, thin, tilted band. Cutting across both bands, into two halves along their length, gives a WSS of 905. The true split gives 1716. k-means minimizes WSS, so it picks the wrong cut. Scaling does not help: the bands are tilted, so both variables have the same spread already. (Class 8’s Gaussian mixture models can fit long, tilted clusters.)
Rings and moons: single linkage wins. Single linkage joins two groups when their two closest points are near. It follows a chain of near neighbours around a curve. The same behaviour makes it fail on round groups: a few points between groups are enough to chain them together.

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
6. Reading a dendrogram
Hierarchical clustering builds a tree. Each merge is drawn at the height of the distance between the two groups it joins. Cutting the tree with a horizontal line gives the clusters: each branch that the line crosses is one cluster.
These 30 points come from three groups. The numbers on the points match the leaves of the tree.

library(shiny)
library(bslib)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)
ctr <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(3, 0.5), c(1.2, 3))
d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(30, ctr[rep(1:3, each = 10), 1], 0.55),
                x2 = rnorm(30, ctr[rep(1:3, each = 10), 2], 0.55),
                id = 1:30)
D <- dist(d[, c("x1", "x2")])
pal <- c("#3B4992", "#EE0000", "#008B45", "#631879", "#E69F00", "#008280",
         "#BB0021", "#5F559B")

ui <- page_sidebar(
  sidebar = sidebar(
    radioButtons("link", "linkage", choices = c("complete", "average", "single", "ward.D2")),
    sliderInput("K", "cut into K clusters", min = 1, max = 8, value = 3)
  ),
  layout_columns(col_widths = c(7, 5),
    plotOutput("tree", height = "560px"),
    plotOutput("scatter", height = "560px"))
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  h <- reactive(hclust(D, method = input$link))
  output$tree <- renderPlot({
    hc <- h()
    heights <- sort(hc$height, decreasing = TRUE)
    cut_at <- if (input$K == 1) max(hc$height) * 1.05 else mean(heights[c(input$K - 1, input$K)])
    par(mar = c(2, 4, 3, 1), cex = 1.1)
    plot(hc, hang = -1, main = sprintf("%s linkage: cut at height %.2f", input$link, cut_at),
         xlab = "", sub = "", ylab = "merge height")
    abline(h = cut_at, col = "#EE0000", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
    if (input$K > 1) rect.hclust(hc, k = input$K, border = pal[1:input$K])
  }, res = 96)
  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    cl <- cutree(h(), input$K)
    # colour clusters in the left-to-right order of the tree, to match the boxes
    ord <- unique(cl[h()$order])
    d$cluster <- factor(match(cl, ord))
    ggplot(d, aes(x1, x2, colour = cluster, label = id)) +
      geom_point(size = 7, alpha = 0.35) + geom_text(size = 4, colour = "black") +
      scale_colour_manual(values = pal) + coord_equal() +
      labs(title = sprintf("K = %d", input$K)) +
      theme_bw(base_size = 15) + theme(legend.position = "none")
  }, res = 96)
}

Things to try:

Move the cut. One tree gives every \(K\) from 1 to 30. You choose \(K\) after the fit, by choosing the height of the cut.
Look for a long vertical gap. With Ward linkage, the three groups merge far above everything else. A cut anywhere in that long gap gives the same three clusters, and here they match the true groups (one point off). This is the “longest vertical line” rule from the slides. Complete linkage also shows a gap at three clusters, but a shorter one, and its three clusters misplace 4 points.
Read heights, not left-to-right order. Two leaves next to each other on the axis are not always close. Only the height where their branches join tells you how far apart they are.
Compare the linkages. Single linkage makes a flat, chained tree: below the top merge, the merge heights are small and close together, so there is no clear place to cut. Ward’s merge heights are on another scale (they grow with the increase in WSS), so compare the shape of the trees, not the numbers.

title: Class 7/Lab 1: Seeing k-means
text:
Things worth remembering

Lloyd’s algorithm never increases WSS, so it always stops. But it stops at a local minimum. Use nstart = 25 or more, and set a seed.
Distance depends on units. A variable with a large spread dominates, even when it carries no information. Standardize first.
No single tool chooses \(K\). The silhouette cannot say “no clusters”. The gap statistic gives up when groups overlap. Use them together, and look at the clusters.
k-means finds round groups of similar size. For long, curved, or nested groups, it gives a confident but wrong answer. Hierarchical clustering with a suitable linkage, or the mixture models of Class 8, can do better.

A note on caret
In earlier labs, caret::train() fit every model. train() tunes a model against an outcome, and clustering has no outcome. So in this lab, caret does the preprocessing with preProcess(), the same tool that train(..., preProcess = ...) used inside earlier labs. The clustering itself uses kmeans() and hclust() from base R, and silhouette() and clusGap() from the cluster package.

title: Class 7/Lab 2: k-means on Thyroid Patients
text:
The data: thyroid function tests
The data come from 215 patients at a hospital in Belgium (Coomans et al., 1983). Each patient had five blood tests:








Column
Test
What it measures




RT3U
T3-resin uptake (%)
how much thyroid hormone binding capacity is free


T4
total serum thyroxine
the main hormone the thyroid makes


T3
total serum triiodothyronine
the active form of the hormone


TSH
basal TSH
the pituitary’s signal to the thyroid (“make more”)


dTSH
TSH change after a TRH injection
how strongly the pituitary responds



Doctors gave each patient a diagnosis from the full medical record: Normal (euthyroid), Hyper (overactive thyroid), or Hypo (underactive thyroid). We hide the diagnosis from the algorithm, and we use it only at the end to check.








150 of the 215 patients are normal. The two disease groups are small (35 and 30 patients).

What a clinician expects
A clinician reads these tests together. In hyperthyroidism, T4 and T3 are high, and the pituitary stops sending TSH. In hypothyroidism, T4 is low, and the pituitary sends a lot of TSH to push the thyroid harder. The median values per group show this:








If k-means finds groups like these, it found real clinical structure.


Scales and shapes








Two problems are visible:

The scales are different. The SD of RT3U is 13.2. The SD of T3 is 1.4. k-means uses Euclidean distance, so a difference of 10 in RT3U counts the same as a difference of 10 in T3. But 10 units of T3 is the whole range of the data.
TSH and dTSH are very skewed. Most patients have a TSH near 1, and a few have values above 30. Those few patients are far from everyone else, and they pull the centroids toward them.

title: Class 7/Lab 2: k-means on Thyroid Patients
text:
Try it yourself
1. Four clusters. Re-run k-means with centers = 4. Which group does the fourth cluster split? Profile the clusters on the original units (copy the profile code from Part 1). Is the new split clinically meaningful, or does k-means cut a continuous group in two?








2. Fewer tests. A clinic often orders only T4 and TSH. Cluster with those two columns only (use z[, c("T4", "TSH")]). How many patients does each diagnosis lose, compared with all five tests?








3. Scaled only, then the silhouette. Re-run the silhouette loop from Part 3 on z_scale (centered and scaled, no Yeo-Johnson). Which \(K\) does it pick now? Compare with the table in Part 1: the preprocessing with the better match to the diagnoses has the lower silhouette. What does this tell you about using the silhouette to choose the preprocessing?

title: Class 7/Lab 2: k-means on Thyroid Patients
text:
Things worth remembering

Preprocessing is part of the model. Raw, scaled, and transformed data gave three different clusterings. Always scale. Check for skew, and transform when one tail dominates.
Use many starts and set a seed. One start can stop at a worse local minimum, and nothing warns you.
The tools for choosing \(K\) often disagree. The elbow, the silhouette, and the gap statistic each answer a geometric question. Use them to find a short list, then decide with the profiles and with someone who knows the domain.
Profile your clusters. A table of cluster medians on the original units is what turns “cluster 2” into “hypothyroid”.
Linkage matters. Single linkage chains. Ward behaves most like k-means.
